1 Chronicles 1: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 1 (1 Chronicles 1:1).
1 Chronicles 2: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 2 (1 Chronicles 2:1).
1 Chronicles 3: David's sons born at Hebron and Jerusalem are listed, then the kings of Judah, then Jehoiachin's descendants after the exile.
1 Chronicles 4: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 4 (1 Chronicles 4:1).
1 Chronicles 5: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 5 (1 Chronicles 5:1).
1 Chronicles 6: The Levite families are listed, including the high priests down to the exile, the temple singers, and the Levites' cities.
1 Chronicles 7: The genealogies of Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher are given, several in military census form.
1 Chronicles 8: The genealogy of Benjamin centers on Gibeon and on Saul's descendants.
1 Chronicles 9: The chapter lists those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon, with the duties of priests, Levites, and gatekeepers.
1 Chronicles 10: Saul dies on mount Gilboa (as in 1 Samuel 31), about 1010 BC.
1 Chronicles 11: David is anointed king over Israel at Hebron and takes Jebus, which becomes Jerusalem, the city of David (as in 2 Samuel 5).
1 Chronicles 12: The chapter lists the men who joined David at Ziklag and at Hebron.
1 Chronicles 13: David tries to bring the ark from Kirjathjearim, but Uzza dies (as in 2 Samuel 6).
1 Chronicles 14: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 14 (1 Chronicles 14:1).
1 Chronicles 15: The Levites carry the ark into Jerusalem with singers and instruments.
1 Chronicles 16: The ark is placed in a tent in Jerusalem, while the tabernacle stays at Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16:39). David's psalm uses parts of Psalms 105, 96, and 106.
1 Chronicles 17: Nathan brings God's promise to David of a lasting house (as in 2 Samuel 7).
1 Chronicles 18: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 18 (1 Chronicles 18:1).
1 Chronicles 19: War with Ammon and its Syrian allies follows the shaming of David's messengers (as in 2 Samuel 10).
1 Chronicles 20: Joab takes Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, and David's men kill Philistine giants from Gath.
1 Chronicles 21: David's census brings a plague. He buys the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite in Jerusalem (as in 2 Samuel 24).
1 Chronicles 22: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 22 (1 Chronicles 22:1).
1 Chronicles 23: David, old, makes Solomon king and counts the Levites from thirty years old and upward: 38,000 (1 Chronicles 23:3).
1 Chronicles 24: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 24 (1 Chronicles 24:1).
1 Chronicles 25: The temple musicians from the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun are organized into twenty-four courses.
1 Chronicles 26: The gatekeepers, treasurers, and officers are assigned their posts.
1 Chronicles 27: Twelve army divisions serve one month each, followed by lists of tribal leaders and royal officials.
1 Chronicles 28: This material is set in the remembered history of Israel and Judah, with the people and places named in 1 Chronicles 28 (1 Chronicles 28:1).
1 Chronicles 29: The leaders give for the temple, Solomon is made king a second time, and David dies after forty years, seven at Hebron and thirty-three at Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 29:27).
2 Chronicles 1: Solomon sacrifices at Gibeon, where the tabernacle and bronze altar still stand, and asks for wisdom (as in 1 Kings 3).
2 Chronicles 2: Solomon arranges with Huram king of Tyre for cedar and craftsmen.
2 Chronicles 3: Solomon builds the temple on mount Moriah, at Ornan's threshingfloor, in the second month of his fourth year (2 Chronicles 3:1–2).
2 Chronicles 4: The bronze altar, molten sea, and vessels are cast in clay in the Jordan plain (2 Chronicles 4:17).
2 Chronicles 5: The ark is brought into the temple at the feast in the seventh month (2 Chronicles 5:3).
2 Chronicles 6: Solomon prays at the dedication from a bronze platform in the temple court (as in 1 Kings 8).
2 Chronicles 7: Fire falls on the sacrifices, and the feast lasts seven days followed by seven more (2 Chronicles 7:8–9).
2 Chronicles 8: After twenty years of building, Solomon builds cities and sends ships from Eziongeber to Ophir.
2 Chronicles 9: The queen of Sheba visits. Solomon reigns forty years and dies (2 Chronicles 9:30).
2 Chronicles 10: The northern tribes reject Rehoboam at Shechem, about 930 BC (as in 1 Kings 12).
2 Chronicles 11: Rehoboam fortifies cities in Judah, and priests and Levites from the north move to Jerusalem.
2 Chronicles 12: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak of Egypt invades with 1,200 chariots and takes the temple treasures, about 925 BC.
2 Chronicles 13: Abijah of Judah defeats Jeroboam of Israel in the hill country of Ephraim.
2 Chronicles 14: Asa of Judah defeats Zerah the Ethiopian and pursues him to Gerar.
2 Chronicles 15: Azariah the prophet speaks, and Asa gathers Judah in Jerusalem in the third month of his fifteenth year (2 Chronicles 15:10).
2 Chronicles 16: In Asa's thirty-sixth year, Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah, and Asa pays Benhadad of Syria to attack Israel.
2 Chronicles 17: Jehoshaphat sends officials and Levites to teach the law in the cities of Judah, in the 9th century BC.
2 Chronicles 18: Jehoshaphat allies with Ahab of Israel against Syria at Ramothgilead, about 853 BC (as in 1 Kings 22).
2 Chronicles 19: Jehoshaphat appoints judges in Judah's fortified cities and in Jerusalem.
2 Chronicles 20: Moab, Ammon, and others invade from beyond the Dead Sea to Engedi. Jehoshaphat's army goes out to the wilderness of Tekoa.
2 Chronicles 21: Jehoram of Judah, married to Ahab's daughter, loses Edom and Libnah in revolts.
2 Chronicles 22: Ahaziah of Judah is killed in Jehu's revolt about 841 BC, and his mother Athaliah seizes the throne.
2 Chronicles 23: Jehoiada the priest crowns Joash in the temple, and Athaliah is killed.
2 Chronicles 24: Joash repairs the temple with a chest for offerings. After Jehoiada's death, Zechariah son of Jehoiada is stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–21).
2 Chronicles 25: Amaziah defeats Edom in the valley of salt, then is defeated by Joash of Israel.
2 Chronicles 26: Uzziah reigns fifty-two years in the 8th century BC (2 Chronicles 26:3) and is struck with leprosy. Isaiah sees his vision "in the year that king Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1).
2 Chronicles 27: Jotham reigns sixteen years and makes Ammon pay tribute.
2 Chronicles 28: Ahaz is attacked by Syria, Israel, Edom, and the Philistines and asks Tilgathpilneser of Assyria for help, in the 730s BC.
2 Chronicles 29: In the first month of his first year, Hezekiah opens the temple doors and cleanses the temple (2 Chronicles 29:3, 17), in the late 8th century BC.
2 Chronicles 30: Hezekiah invites Israel and Judah, from Beersheba to Dan, to keep Passover in Jerusalem in the second month.
2 Chronicles 31: The people destroy high places, and tithes are brought to the temple from the third to the seventh month (2 Chronicles 31:7).
2 Chronicles 32: Sennacherib invades in 701 BC. Hezekiah stops the springs and brings water into the city (2 Chronicles 32:30); his tunnel under Jerusalem, with its Siloam inscription, still exists.
2 Chronicles 33: Manasseh reigns fifty-five years and is taken to Babylon by the Assyrian army, then returns to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 33:11–13).
2 Chronicles 34: Josiah begins to seek God at sixteen and purges idolatry at twenty; the book of the law is found in his eighteenth year, 622 BC (2 Chronicles 34:3, 8).
2 Chronicles 35: Josiah keeps Passover and dies at Megiddo in 609 BC fighting Necho of Egypt. Jeremiah laments him (2 Chronicles 35:25).
2 Chronicles 36: Judah's last kings fall to Babylon, and Jerusalem is burned in 586 BC. The book ends with Cyrus's decree of 538 BC.
